topics.title: What is NXC/NetExec
topics.content: NetExec (NXC) is the modern, actively maintained successor to CrackMapExec (CME). It is a network service exploitation tool used by penetration testers and red teamers to automate the assessment of large Active Directory environments. NXC authenticates to multiple network services (SMB, LDAP, WinRM, RDP, SSH, FTP, MSSQL, VNC, WMI), enumerates information, sprays credentials, executes commands, and dumps secrets from a single command-line interface. The original CrackMapExec was created by byt3bl33d3r (Marcello Salvati) and became the standard for AD pentesting. In late 2023, the project was forked and renamed to NetExec by the community under the Pennyw0rth organization on GitHub because the original CME repository was archived. All modern usage should use the 'nxc' command, not 'crackmapexec' or 'cme'. The config directory changed from ~/.cme/ to ~/.nxc/ and the database command from 'cmedb' to 'nxcdb'.

topics.title: NXC Installation
topics.content: NXC can be installed through several methods depending on your platform. On Kali Linux 2024 and later, NetExec is included in the default repositories and can be installed via 'sudo apt update && sudo apt install netexec'. The recommended installation method for non-Kali systems is pipx ('pipx install netexec') which creates an isolated virtual environment. You can also use pip ('pip install netexec') though this may conflict with system packages. For the latest development version, clone from GitHub ('git clone https://github.com/Pennyw0rth/NetExec.git') and install locally with 'pipx install .'. After installation, verify with 'nxc --version'. The configuration directory is ~/.nxc/ which contains the database, logs, and module configurations.

topics.title: NXC Basic Syntax and Structure
topics.content: Every NXC command follows the pattern: nxc <protocol> <target(s)> [options]. The protocol is the service to target (smb, ldap, winrm, rdp, ssh, ftp, mssql, vnc, wmi). The target can be a single IP, CIDR range, IP range, hostname, or file containing targets. Common authentication options include -u for username, -p for password, -H for NTLM hash, -d for domain, --local-auth for local authentication, and -k for Kerberos. Multiple usernames or passwords can be specified with multiple -u or -p flags, or by providing files. Target specification supports single IPs (192.168.1.10), CIDR notation (192.168.1.0/24), ranges (192.168.1.1-50), and files (targets.txt with one target per line). The --port flag overrides the default port, -t sets the thread count, and --timeout sets the connection timeout in seconds.

topics.title: Understanding NXC Output Symbols
topics.content: NXC uses three primary symbols in its output to indicate results. The [+] symbol (green) indicates success — a successful authentication or operation. When [+] is followed by (Pwn3d!), it means the authenticated user has local administrator privileges on the target host. For SMB this means access to ADMIN$ or C$ shares; for WinRM it means PowerShell Remoting access; for MSSQL it means sysadmin privileges. The [-] symbol (red) indicates failure — a failed authentication attempt. Common failure status codes include STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE (wrong credentials), STATUS_ACCOUNT_LOCKED_OUT (too many failed attempts), STATUS_ACCOUNT_DISABLED (disabled account), STATUS_PASSWORD_EXPIRED (expired password), and STATUS_PASSWORD_MUST_CHANGE (must change at next logon). The [*] symbol (blue) provides informational output such as host details, OS version, domain name, SMB signing status, and enumeration results. The (Pwn3d!) flag is the most critical indicator — it means you can execute commands, dump secrets, and fully compromise the host.

topics.title: Protocol Modules Overview
topics.content: NXC supports nine protocol modules, each targeting a specific network service. SMB (port 445) is the most versatile — it handles file share enumeration, user/group enumeration, credential attacks, command execution via multiple methods, and secret dumping. LDAP (port 389/636) queries Active Directory for users, groups, trusts, computer objects, and supports Kerberoasting and AS-REP roasting. WinRM (port 5985/5986) enables PowerShell Remoting and command execution on hosts where WinRM is enabled. RDP (port 3389) checks Remote Desktop Protocol access and can take screenshots. SSH (port 22) authenticates and executes commands on Linux/Unix systems and network devices. FTP (port 21) checks FTP authentication and anonymous access. MSSQL (port 1433) targets Microsoft SQL Server for authentication, query execution, and xp_cmdshell command execution. VNC (port 5900) checks VNC authentication. WMI (port 135) uses Windows Management Instrumentation for command execution and queries. Each protocol has its own set of modules and capabilities accessible via 'nxc <protocol> --help'.

topics.title: Target Specification and Authentication
topics.content: NXC supports flexible target specification: single IPs (192.168.1.10), multiple IPs space-separated (192.168.1.10 192.168.1.11), CIDR ranges (192.168.1.0/24), IP ranges (192.168.1.1-50), hostnames (dc01.corp.local), and files containing targets one per line (targets.txt). Authentication supports domain credentials (-u user -p pass -d DOMAIN), local credentials (-u user -p pass --local-auth), NTLM hashes (-u user -H 'LM:NT' or -u user -H 'NT_only'), Kerberos tickets (-k --use-kcache with KRB5CCNAME environment variable), null sessions (-u '' -p ''), and guest access (-u guest -p ''). Domain authentication is the default; if -d is omitted, NXC uses the domain reported by the target. Local authentication (--local-auth) checks against the local SAM database instead of Active Directory — essential when using credentials from SAM dumps or targeting workgroup machines. Multiple usernames and passwords can be specified with repeated -u/-p flags or via files. The --no-bruteforce flag pairs credentials line-by-line instead of trying all combinations.

topics.title: SMB Host Discovery and OS Fingerprinting
topics.content: Running NXC SMB against a target range without credentials performs unauthenticated SMB enumeration, revealing valuable information about every host that responds on port 445. The output line format is: SMB IP PORT HOSTNAME [*] OS_VERSION (name:HOSTNAME) (domain:DOMAIN) (signing:True/False) (SMBv1:True/False). The OS version field shows the exact Windows version and build number (e.g., 'Windows Server 2019 Build 17763 x64' or 'Windows 10 Build 19041 x64'). The signing field is critical: signing:True means SMB signing is required (relay attacks blocked, typically domain controllers), while signing:False means signing is not required (vulnerable to NTLM relay). The SMBv1 field indicates whether the legacy SMBv1 protocol is enabled (potential EternalBlue vulnerability, MS17-010). Domain controllers can usually be identified by signing:True and 'Server' in the OS string. Use --gen-relay-list to automatically generate a file containing only IPs with SMB signing disabled.

topics.title: Share Enumeration
topics.content: The --shares flag enumerates network shares on the target and reports the current user's permissions on each share. Output shows the share name, permissions (READ, WRITE, or READ,WRITE), and remark/description. Default administrative shares include ADMIN$ (Remote Admin — maps to C:\Windows), C$ (Default share — maps to C:\), and IPC$ (Remote IPC — used for named pipe communication). If ADMIN$ or C$ show READ,WRITE permissions, the user has local administrator access. Custom shares like IT_Share, HR_Data, Backups reveal the organization's file sharing structure and may contain sensitive data. Shares can be enumerated across an entire subnet to map all accessible file shares. Null session share enumeration (with empty credentials) may reveal publicly accessible shares on misconfigured systems. The permissions shown reflect the authenticated user's effective access — different users will see different permissions.

topics.title: Share Spidering
topics.content: Share spidering recursively browses the contents of network shares to find files matching specific patterns. NXC provides built-in spidering with the --spider flag (specify the share name) combined with --pattern (regex or comma-separated extensions to match). The --spider-folder flag restricts spidering to a specific subdirectory within the share, and --depth limits recursion depth. Common patterns for finding credentials include 'pass|cred|secret|key|config|backup|password'. Files commonly containing credentials include: web.config and app.config (.NET connection strings), PowerShell scripts (.ps1) and batch files (.bat, .vbs) with hardcoded passwords, unattend.xml and sysprep.xml (deployment credentials), KeePass databases (.kdbx), RDP files (.rdp), certificate files (.pfx, .p12, .pem), and Groups.xml (Group Policy Preferences with AES-encrypted but crackable passwords using gpp-decrypt). For more advanced spidering, use the spider_plus module which indexes all files and outputs structured JSON results. Spider_plus supports exclusions and can be configured to only look at specific file types or skip certain directories.

topics.title: User and Group Enumeration
topics.content: User enumeration (--users) retrieves the list of domain user accounts via the SAM-R protocol or LDAP, showing the username and description for each account. This output is valuable for building a username wordlist for password spraying, identifying service accounts (often prefixed with svc_) which may have SPNs suitable for Kerberoasting, and identifying admin accounts for targeted attacks. Group enumeration (--groups) retrieves domain groups with their member counts — key groups to look for include Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins, Schema Admins, and any custom admin groups like IT_Admins or SQL_Admins. Local group enumeration (--local-groups) shows groups on a specific host, most importantly the local Administrators group membership. These commands require valid domain credentials and are typically run against a domain controller. The --users and --groups flags can be used with the SMB or LDAP protocol modules. For environments where SAM-R enumeration is restricted by GPO, RID brute forcing (--rid-brute) provides an alternative user enumeration method.

topics.title: Session and Logged-On User Enumeration
topics.content: Session enumeration (--sessions) reveals which users have active SMB sessions on the target host, showing the source IP address and the domain\username of each connected user. This is valuable for identifying where high-privilege users (domain admins, service accounts) are currently connected, which helps plan credential theft attacks — if a domain admin has an active session on a server, dumping LSASS on that server will yield their credentials. Logged-on user enumeration (--loggedon-users) shows users who are interactively logged into the target host, including their logon server. Both commands can be run across subnets to map privileged user activity network-wide. The combination of session and loggedon-users data creates a map of 'who is where' — essential for targeted lateral movement. Running these across the entire subnet identifies admin workstations and shows which servers domain admins regularly access. This information directly informs which hosts to target for credential dumping.

topics.title: Password Policy Enumeration
topics.content: The --pass-pol flag retrieves the domain password policy from the target, which is essential information before any password spraying campaign. The output includes: minimum password length, password history length, maximum password age, password complexity requirements, minimum password age, Account Lockout Threshold (number of failed attempts before lockout), Reset Account Lockout Counter (time before the failed attempt counter resets), and Locked Account Duration (how long a locked account stays locked). The most critical fields for spray safety are the lockout threshold and reset counter. Safe spraying rule: never exceed (threshold - 2) attempts per reset period. For example, with a threshold of 5 and a 30-minute reset, try at most 3 passwords per 35-minute window. If the lockout threshold is 0, there is no lockout policy and you can spray more aggressively (but this is rare in production environments). Always retrieve the password policy before spraying — locking out production accounts will end your engagement early and damage your reputation.

topics.title: RID Brute Forcing
topics.content: RID (Relative Identifier) brute forcing enumerates users and groups by cycling through Security Identifier (SID) values. Each domain object has a SID composed of the domain SID plus a unique RID. Well-known RIDs include 500 (Administrator), 501 (Guest), 502 (krbtgt), 512 (Domain Admins), 513 (Domain Users), 514 (Domain Guests), 515 (Domain Computers), 516 (Domain Controllers). Custom user accounts typically start from RID 1000+. The --rid-brute flag accepts an optional maximum RID value (default is around 4000). For larger domains, increase this: --rid-brute 10000 or --rid-brute 20000. RID brute forcing is especially valuable when SAM-R enumeration is blocked by Group Policy (a common hardening measure), when you only have a null session or guest access, and when you need to discover users that --users might miss. The output shows each RID, the domain\username, and the account type (SidTypeUser for user accounts, SidTypeGroup for groups). This technique works through the LSARPC named pipe and may succeed even when other enumeration methods are restricted.

topics.title: SMB Signing and Relay Target Identification
topics.content: SMB signing (message signing) is a security feature that adds a cryptographic signature to each SMB message, preventing man-in-the-middle attacks and NTLM relay. In NXC output, signing:True means SMB signing is required — the host cannot be a target for NTLM relay attacks. Signing:False means signing is not required — the host is vulnerable to relay. By default, domain controllers require signing while member servers and workstations do not. NXC's --gen-relay-list flag automatically generates a file containing only IPs where signing is disabled, ready to use with ntlmrelayx. The relay attack workflow: 1) Use NXC to generate the relay target list, 2) Start Responder to capture NTLM authentication, 3) Start ntlmrelayx with the relay target list, 4) Optionally use NXC's PetitPotam module to coerce authentication from a high-privilege account. If the captured authentication belongs to a user who is admin on a relay target, you get code execution. This is one of the most reliable initial access techniques on internal penetration tests because SMB signing is disabled by default on most Windows systems except DCs.
